lessonTitle: Signal Transduction and Tolerance: Second Messengers, Desensitisation and Dependence

blocks.text: A woman with chronic cancer pain finds that the morphine dose that once controlled her pain now barely touches it, so her dose has been raised several times. When she misses a day, she sweats, shakes and has diarrhoea. Her receptors, signalling pathways and brain circuits have adapted to the drug. Understanding how a receptor signal is generated, and how cells dial it down, explains why the same dose can have less effect over time.

blocks.markdown: When a ligand binds a receptor, the signal must be relayed into the cell and amplified. This is **signal transduction**. For the largest receptor family, the **G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)**, the receptor activates a heterotrimeric G protein (alpha, beta and gamma subunits), which in turn regulates an effector enzyme or channel that generates a **second messenger**. The second messenger activates protein kinases, which phosphorylate target proteins and produce the cellular response.

blocks.title: G proteins and second messengers
blocks.text: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP (cAMP). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP. Gq activates phospholipase C, which cleaves PIP2 into inositol trisphosphate (IP3, releases intracellular calcium) and diacylglycerol (DAG, activates protein kinase C). cAMP is broken down by phosphodiesterases (PDEs).

blocks.caption: Major GPCR signalling pathways with clinical examples.
rows: Heart: increased rate and force; airway: smooth muscle relaxation
Reduced heart rate; reduced transmitter release
Alpha-2 adrenoceptor, M2 muscarinic, mu opioid
IP3 and DAG; intracellular calcium rises

blocks.title: Tracing a beta-1 signal in the heart
blocks.prompt: Trace the sequence of events from noradrenaline binding a cardiac beta-1 receptor to an increased force of contraction.

steps.text: Noradrenaline binds the beta-1 receptor, which changes shape and activates the associated Gs protein (GDP exchanged for GTP on the alpha subunit).
The Gs alpha subunit stimulates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cyclic AMP (cAMP), the second messenger.
cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates proteins including the L-type calcium channel and phospholamban.

More calcium enters and is released and re-uptaken more rapidly, so contraction is stronger and faster. The signal is switched off when the G protein hydrolyses GTP and phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down to AMP.

blocks.answer: Ligand, receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA, phosphorylation of calcium handling proteins, stronger contraction

blocks.caption: n1, n2 and n3 are the numbers of molecules activated at each successive step of the cascade. Because each step is catalytic, one ligand binding event can generate many second messenger molecules.

blocks.title: Why cascades matter
blocks.text: Signal amplification explains why a small number of occupied receptors can produce a full response (spare receptors) and why drugs that act on enzymes in the cascade, such as phosphodiesterase inhibitors like theophylline, can modify cell responses without touching the receptor.

blocks.markdown: **Desensitisation and down-regulation.** Continued exposure to an agonist makes cells less responsive. **Desensitisation** occurs within seconds to minutes. For many GPCRs, receptor kinases (GRKs) phosphorylate the occupied receptor, which then binds **beta-arrestin**, uncoupling it from the G protein. Receptors may then be internalised in vesicles and either recycled to the surface (recovery) or sent to lysosomes. **Down-regulation** is a longer-term fall in the total number of receptors (over hours to days) through increased degradation and reduced synthesis. Up-regulation, an increase in receptor number, may follow prolonged antagonist exposure, which can contribute to rebound effects when the drug stops.

blocks.title: Quantifying down-regulation
blocks.prompt: Receptor binding assays show a receptor density of 250 fmol/mg protein before prolonged agonist exposure and 150 fmol/mg after. Calculate the percentage down-regulation, and the likely consequence for the dose-response curve. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: Calculate the fall in receptor number.
Express as a percentage of the original density.

Fewer receptors means fewer occupied receptors at a given agonist concentration. If receptor reserve is limited, the maximal response falls; where spare receptors exist, the curve first shifts to the right (a higher concentration is needed).
Clinically, the same dose gives a smaller effect, the hallmark of tolerance.

blocks.answer: 40% down-regulation; reduced response so that higher doses are required for the same effect

blocks.caption: Tolerance, dependence and tachyphylaxis distinguished.
rows: Progressively reduced response to a drug with repeated use, so higher doses are needed
Adaptation such that stopping the drug produces a withdrawal syndrome; physical dependence is distinct from compulsive use (addiction)
Opioid withdrawal, alcohol, benzodiazepines, beta-blocker rebound
Very rapid tolerance developing after a few doses, within minutes to hours
Repeated doses of indirectly acting sympathomimetics such as ephedrine (store depletion); glyceryl trinitrate

items: Tolerance can arise from desensitisation, receptor down-regulation, depletion of mediators, increased metabolism (for example enzyme induction) or homeostatic adaptation.
Physical dependence is not the same as addiction; patients on long-term opioids for pain may be dependent but not addicted.
Withdrawal effects are generally the opposite of the drug's effect, as the adapted system is unopposed.
Abrupt cessation of drugs that cause dependence (opioids, benzodiazepines, beta-blockers) should be avoided; taper gradually.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the terms
blocks.text: Tolerance is reduced drug effect; dependence is a withdrawal state on stopping. Both can occur together, and neither means the patient is misusing the drug.

points: GPCR signals pass through G proteins (Gs raises cAMP, Gi lowers it, Gq raises IP3 and calcium) to kinases that phosphorylate target proteins, amplifying the original signal.
Desensitisation is rapid uncoupling of the receptor (phosphorylation and arrestin binding), while down-regulation is a longer-term loss of receptor number.
Tolerance is reduced response with repeated dosing, tachyphylaxis is very rapid tolerance, and dependence is adaptation revealed as a withdrawal syndrome when the drug stops.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes signalling through a Gs-coupled receptor?

options.text: Receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A
Receptor, Gq, phospholipase C, IP3, calcium
Receptor, Gi, adenylyl cyclase inhibited, cAMP falls
Receptor, ion channel opens, kinase cascade

questions.correctOptionText: Receptor, Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP and activate PKA.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this describes the Gq pathway.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: this describes the Gi pathway.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: this does not describe a GPCR pathway.

questions.explanation: Gs-coupled receptors, such as the beta-adrenoceptors, stimulate adenylyl cyclase to produce cAMP, which activates protein kinase A. Gq and Gi use different effectors.

questions.stem: Salbutamol relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Which intracellular change is part of the mechanism?

options.text: Increased cAMP and activation of protein kinase A
Decreased cAMP via Gi
Increased IP3 and calcium release
Increased phosphodiesterase activity

questions.correctOptionText: Increased cAMP and activation of protein kinase A

distractorRationale.a: Correct: beta-2 stimulation raises cAMP, activating PKA and relaxing smooth muscle.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: beta-2 receptors couple to Gs, not Gi.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: IP3 and calcium promote contraction via Gq.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: more phosphodiesterase would lower cAMP.

questions.explanation: Beta-2 agonists act through Gs to raise cAMP, activating PKA, which promotes smooth muscle relaxation. Pathways that raise IP3 and calcium instead promote contraction.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes signalling when noradrenaline stimulates alpha-1 adrenoceptors on vascular smooth muscle?

options.text: Gq, phospholipase C, IP3 releases intracellular calcium, contraction
Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, relaxation
Gi, reduced cAMP, relaxation
Direct opening of a sodium channel by noradrenaline

questions.correctOptionText: Gq, phospholipase C, IP3 releases intracellular calcium, contraction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: alpha-1 receptors couple to Gq, increasing IP3, calcium and contraction.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this is the beta pathway.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: Gi is not used by alpha-1 receptors.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: alpha-1 receptors are not ion channels.

questions.explanation: Alpha-1 receptors use Gq to activate phospholipase C, producing IP3 and DAG. IP3 releases calcium from stores, causing smooth muscle contraction and vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: Theophylline is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor used in some patients with airway disease. How does this help to relax bronchial smooth muscle?

options.text: It slows the breakdown of cAMP so that cAMP accumulates
It increases the synthesis of IP3
It blocks Gs proteins
It activates alpha-1 receptors

questions.correctOptionText: It slows the breakdown of cAMP so that cAMP accumulates

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inhibition of phosphodiesterase prolongs cAMP signalling.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: blocking Gs would reduce cAMP.

questions.explanation: Phosphodiesterases degrade cAMP, so inhibiting them raises its level and enhances PKA-mediated relaxation. This acts downstream of the receptor.

questions.stem: In a signalling cascade, one activated receptor activates 10 G proteins, each G protein activates 1 adenylyl cyclase molecule, and each adenylyl cyclase produces 50 cAMP molecules. Calculate the number of cAMP molecules generated per activated receptor.
questions.explanation: Amplification at each step multiplies: 10 x 1 x 50 = 500 cAMP molecules per activated receptor. This illustrates how a small receptor signal is greatly amplified.

questions.stem: A cell line has a receptor density of 400 fmol/mg protein. After 48 hours of continuous agonist exposure it is 240 fmol/mg. Calculate the percentage down-regulation of the receptor.
questions.explanation: The fall is 400 - 240 = 160 fmol/mg, and 160 / 400 = 0.40, so 40% of receptors have been lost. This reduces the cell's response to the agonist.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes receptor desensitisation from down-regulation?

options.text: Desensitisation is rapid uncoupling of the receptor from its G protein, whereas down-regulation is a slower loss of receptor number
Desensitisation is loss of receptors and down-regulation is receptor phosphorylation
Both occur only after months of exposure
Neither involves changes at the receptor

questions.correctOptionText: Desensitisation is rapid uncoupling of the receptor from its G protein, whereas down-regulation is a slower loss of receptor number

distractorRationale.a: Correct: desensitisation takes seconds to minutes (phosphorylation, arrestin), down-regulation takes hours to days.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: desensitisation occurs within seconds to minutes.

questions.explanation: Receptor phosphorylation and arrestin binding quickly uncouple the receptor from the G protein (desensitisation), while degradation and reduced synthesis lower the number of receptors over hours to days (down-regulation). Recovery from desensitisation is therefore quick once the agonist is removed, whereas recovery from down-regulation requires new receptor synthesis.

questions.stem: A patient in a coronary care unit receiving repeated doses of an indirectly acting sympathomimetic finds the pressor response is much smaller after the third dose given over two hours. Which term best describes this?

options.text: Tachyphylaxis
Physical dependence
Idiosyncratic reaction
Receptor up-regulation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: very rapid loss of response over a few doses, as stores of releasable noradrenaline are depleted.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: dependence refers to withdrawal on stopping.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: this is an expected pharmacological phenomenon.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: up-regulation would increase, not reduce, response.

questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is tolerance that develops within minutes to hours. With indirectly acting sympathomimetics the response falls because stores of noradrenaline in nerve terminals are depleted.

questions.stem: Distinguish tolerance, dependence and tachyphylaxis, giving an example of each.
markingGuide: Tolerance: reduced response to repeated dosing so higher doses are needed; develops over days to weeks; example opioids or benzodiazepines
Tachyphylaxis: very rapid tolerance within minutes to hours; example ephedrine, or nitrates
Dependence: adaptation such that stopping the drug causes a withdrawal syndrome
Physical dependence differs from addiction (compulsive use despite harm)
Withdrawal features usually opposite to the drug's effect (for example opioid withdrawal with diarrhoea, sweating and agitation)
Mechanisms: receptor desensitisation, down-regulation, depletion of mediators or enzyme induction
questions.explanation: The terms differ in time course and in what they describe: a lower response, a very fast lower response, or a withdrawal state. They can coexist in one patient.

questions.stem: Trace a G-protein-coupled receptor signal through cAMP to a cellular response, and explain how continued agonist exposure leads to reduced responsiveness.
markingGuide: Agonist binds receptor, which activates Gs (GTP replaces GDP on the alpha subunit)
Gs alpha stimulates adenylyl cyclase converting ATP to cAMP
cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates target proteins giving the cellular response (for example heart: calcium handling proteins, increased contractility)
Signal terminated by GTP hydrolysis and phosphodiesterase breakdown of cAMP
Desensitisation: receptor phosphorylation by GRK, arrestin binding, uncoupling and internalisation (minutes)
Down-regulation: reduced receptor number through degradation and reduced synthesis (hours to days), so less response
questions.explanation: The cascade amplifies a receptor event into a cell response through second messengers. Feedback on the receptor then reduces the response when the agonist is present continuously.
